title: Food & drink
goal: Name everyday South Indian foods, say what you want and what you like, and order in a restaurant.
intro: Food is at the heart of Tamil life — from the morning **இட்லி** and filter **காபி** to a full rice meal served on a banana leaf. In this unit you will learn the key **dative-subject** pattern: in Tamil you don't say 'I want' or 'I like', but 'to me … is wanted' (**எனக்கு … வேணும்**) and 'to me … is pleasing' (**எனக்கு … பிடிக்கும்**).

vocab.note: spoken: தோச dōsa; initial த is voiced in this word
spoken: பழம் / பளம் paḷam in some areas
also means 'drink alcohol' when used alone
spoken: வேணும் vēṇum; used with dative subject

phrases.en: Two idlis and one dosa, please.

grammar.title: Dative subject: 'I want', 'I like', 'I'm hungry'
grammar.body:
Many feelings and needs are expressed with the experiencer in the **dative case (-க்கு)** and the thing as the grammatical subject:

**எனக்கு காபி வேணும்** — to-me coffee is-wanted → 'I want coffee'
**எனக்கு காபி பிடிக்கும்** — to-me coffee is-pleasing → 'I like coffee'
**எனக்குப் பசிக்குது** — to-me (it) hungers → 'I'm hungry'

The verb doesn't change for person: வேணும், பிடிக்கும் stay the same whoever wants or likes. Negatives: **வேணாம்** 'don't want', **பிடிக்காது** 'don't like'. Questions: வேணுமா? பிடிக்குமா?

(A hard consonant after -க்கு is often doubled in writing — எனக்குப் பசி *enakkup pasi* — this is sandhi; in casual speech it is weak or dropped, and many people leave it out when writing spoken Tamil.)

grammar.title: Ordering politely with குடுங்க
grammar.body:
In restaurants and shops you simply name the item and add **குடுங்க** *kuḍunga* 'please give' (written கொடுங்கள்). Adding **கொஞ்சம்** *konjam* 'a little' softens any request: கொஞ்சம் தண்ணி குடுங்க.

To ask whether something is available, use **இருக்கா?** *irukkā?* 'is there?'. The answer is **இருக்கு** 'there is' or **இல்ல** 'there isn't'. 'Give me … more' is **இன்னும் … குடுங்க**.

dialogue.title: Breakfast at a tiffin centre
dialogue.setting: Tom and his friend Karthik sit down at a busy vegetarian restaurant in the morning.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: There's idli, dosa, pongal and puri.

lines.speaker: Karthik
lines.native: எனக்கு ரெண்டு இட்லி, ஒரு வடை. டாம், உங்களுக்கு?
lines.roman: enakku reṇḍu iḍli, oru vaḍai. Ṭām, ungaḷukku?
lines.en: Two idlis and a vadai for me. Tom, for you?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: எனக்கு ஒரு மசாலா தோசை வேணும். காரமா இருக்குமா?
lines.roman: enakku oru masālā dōsai vēṇum. kāramā irukkumā?
lines.en: I want a masala dosa. Will it be spicy?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: That's fine. I like spicy food!

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: ரொம்ப ருசியா இருக்கு! இன்னும் கொஞ்சம் சாம்பார் குடுங்க.
lines.roman: romba rusiyā irukku! innum konjam sāmbār kuḍunga.
lines.en: It's delicious! A little more sambar, please.

culture: Traditional meals are eaten with the right hand, often from a banana leaf (வாழை இலை). Hosts will keep serving you; say போதும் 'enough' firmly — and folding the leaf towards you signals you have finished and enjoyed the meal. Filter coffee is served in a tumbler and dabarah (டபரா) and 'pulled' between the two to cool and froth it. Many Tamil homes and restaurants are vegetarian (சைவம்); a 'military hotel' is, oddly, a non-vegetarian restaurant.
